result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.compose_all()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Combine any number of graphs with compose(). twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.compose_all()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Combine any number of graphs with compose(). title: >- [Graph.compose_all()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Combine any number of graphs with compose(). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Combine any number of graphs with `compose()`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L51064-L51132){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.compose_all(graphs) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Compose many graphs](../assets/graphs/compose-all.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three graphs on the same nodes A, B, C: base has edge A–B (accent), update1 adds B–C (teal), and update2 adds C–A (violet). compose_all merges nodes and edges by id from left to right, later graphs winning any attribute clash, so the result is the triangle A, B, C with 3 edges, each in the color of the graph that supplied it." width="100%"} Applies `compose()` from left to right, so nodes and edges are merged by ID and, where graphs disagree on attributes, later graphs win. Use it to overlay a series of updates on a base graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [graphs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A non-empty list of graphs with the same directedness. None is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph (a copy, if only one graph is given). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the list is empty or the graphs differ in directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Equivalent to `graphs[0].compose(graphs[1]).compose(graphs[2])...`. Mirrors NetworkX's `compose_all`. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~compose`) : Combine two graphs, letting the other graph's values win. [](`~union_all`) : Combine any number of graphs, keeping the first graph's values. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships in 2024 among the members of a chess club and a climbing club, and `snapshot=2` is the network a year later, with 8 new friendships. Here the 2024 list is followed by a 2026 list, in which three friendships have ended, and by a note that Vik has moved to chess: ::: {#ed35e350 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec updates = [ ec.friends(), ec.friends(snapshot=2) .delete_edge("Dev", "Femi") .delete_edge("Gwen", "Lou") .delete_edge("Rosa", "Sven"), ec.friends().set_node_attrs("club", "Chess", nodes=["Vik"]), ] latest = ec.Graph.compose_all(updates) ``` ::: The updates apply in order, so the last one wins and Vik is in chess. Composing never removes anything, though, so the three friendships that ended are still there, 51 in all: ::: {#d3821a68 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} vik = latest.get_id_from_label("Vik") latest.get_node_attrs("club")[vik], latest.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ('Chess', 51) ``` ::: ::: To drop the lost ties, use `intersection()` or `difference()` with the newer list.
